meta.title: Email Attraction: Get What You Want Every Time You Hit Send
meta.author: Kim Arnold

parts.title: The Value of Essential Email Skills

sentences: **Kim Arnold**'s book on becoming better at **email** communication is crucial because many spend **years** (six on average) buried in their **inbox**.
With little training, people struggle with **inefficient** emails that waste time and cause **frustration**.
Good news—**email** can be incredibly **effective**, saving you time if done **correctly**.

The book aims to help you become "The Big Email Enchilada," turning your email skills into a **superpower** to cut down those six years to even two or one by improving your **communication** strategy.

parts.title: Avoid Emotional Emails & Effective Email Communication

sentences: **Avoid emotional emails**: Before sending emails when **emotional**, wait at least an **hour** to **calm down**.
Consider if the **email** will get **desired results** or just appease **immediate feelings**.
**Read aloud** to check if you'd say it face-to-face and get **impartial advice** to **avoid unnecessary conflict**.
**Effective Communication Tips**: Consider the **recipient's perspective**; think about their **style and preferences**.
Use the **three Ws**: **Who** you're writing to, **What** you want, and **Why** they should care.
Create a **two-way conversation** to engage your reader and avoid being a **"party bore"**.
Use **clear** and **engaging** language rather than stiff language to connect.

parts.title: Emails and Visual Appeal - Drawing Parallels with Gourmet Cuisine

paragraphs.heading: How Emails are Like Gourmet Meals
sentences: **Fancy chefs** have a way of making dishes visually **appealing** before you taste them - your **emails** should do the same.
Just like we judge food **visually**, readers judge emails by how they look at first glance.
A messy email is like a greying steak; unappealing and **forgettable**.
To make emails attractive, **create** spaces and make them **easy** to read with short **sentences** and **paragraphs**.
This attracts readers and helps them focus on your important message.

paragraphs.heading: The Power of White Space in Emails
sentences: Just like a **cavernous lobby**, white space in your emails creates a sense of **calm** and importance.
Too many words create chaos and **overwhelm** - it feels like climbing a "word wall."
**Short** sentences and **generous** spacing make messages **clear** and leave room for **important** information.
This makes your emails **engaging** and easier to handle, turning your writing into a more **effective** communication tool.
Having a clear, concise, and compelling **call-to-action (CTA)** in your emails is important.
It emphasizes that a CTA should ask for **one thing only**, be direct, offer a clear and manageable next step, include a **timeframe**, and ideally be short, preferably one sentence.
Common mistakes include being too vague or **overwhelming** with multiple requests, and solutions on how to improve them are offered.
Key tips include dividing tasks into separate emails, using numbered lists for multiple requests, and always including a strong **verb** and deadline.
Imagine crafting an email and being ready to hit **send**.
Hold on!
Reviewing and editing your email is crucial.
A slip of the keyboard, like missing an ‘l’ in ‘public’, can lead to **embarrassing typos**.
Research indicates typos can make us appear less **intelligent**.
Like dating, people often judge others by their **grammar**, so it’s worth ensuring your email is error-free.
To perfect your email, try these steps: Reading it **out loud** helps spot awkward phrasing or mistakes.
Aim for an email length of about **eighty words**, focusing on the necessary.
Apply the **HEC Hamburger** technique with a **hook**, **explanation**, and **CTA**.
Check its appearance and use tools like **Grammarly** for spellcheck, but do a manual **proofread** too.
Editing enhances your credibility and effectiveness significantly.
